stem: You can see a wooden chair in a lit room. Which statement describes how you see it?

options.text: Light from the lamp reflects off the chair and enters your eye
Your eye sends out rays that strike the chair
The chair produces its own light which reaches your eye
The chair must be hot for you to see it

explanation: Non-luminous objects are seen by diffusely reflecting light from a source into the eye.

stem: Why can you not see around a corner, even in a brightly lit corridor?

options.text: Light travels in straight lines in a uniform medium
Rays from the eye cannot turn corners
Light is absorbed completely by the wall
Light slows down near solid objects

explanation: Rectilinear propagation means light does not bend round an obstacle at everyday scales.

stem: A ray strikes a plane mirror at 30 degrees to the mirror surface. What is the angle of reflection?

options.text: 60 degrees
30 degrees
120 degrees
The ray passes into the mirror and bends

explanation: Angles are measured from the normal, so the angle of incidence is 90 - 30 = 60 degrees, and reflection equals it.

stem: Which quantities always lie in one plane for a reflected ray?

options.text: Incident ray, reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence
Incident ray, refracted ray and the mirror surface
Only the incident and reflected rays
The normal and the mirror surface only

explanation: The second law of reflection states all three lie in the same plane.

stem: You stand 2 m from a plane mirror. How far is your image from you?

options.text: 4 m
2 m
1 m
It depends on the size of the mirror

explanation: The image is 2 m behind the mirror, so it is 4 m from you.

stem: Which set correctly describes the image in a plane mirror?

options.text: Virtual, erect, same size, laterally inverted
Real, erect, same size, formed on the mirror surface
Virtual, inverted, magnified
Real, inverted, diminished

explanation: A plane mirror always gives a virtual, erect, same-sized, laterally inverted image as far behind as the object is in front.

stem: A concave mirror has a radius of curvature of 24 cm. What is its focal length?

options.text: 12 cm
24 cm
48 cm
6 cm

explanation: For a spherical mirror f = R/2 = 12 cm.

stem: The centre of curvature of a concave mirror lies 30 cm from the pole. Where is the principal focus?

options.text: 15 cm from the pole, in front of the mirror
30 cm from the pole, coinciding with the centre of curvature
15 cm behind the mirror
At the pole itself

explanation: F is the midpoint of P and C, so 15 cm in front for a concave mirror.

stem: An object is placed between the pole and the focus of a concave mirror. The image is:

options.text: Virtual, erect and enlarged
Real, inverted and enlarged
Real, inverted and diminished
Formed exactly on the mirror surface

explanation: Inside the focus the reflected rays diverge, so only their extensions meet: a virtual, erect, magnified image. This is the shaving-mirror case.

stem: An object sits at the centre of curvature of a concave mirror. The image is:

options.text: At C, real, inverted and the same size
At F, real, inverted and diminished
Behind the mirror, virtual and erect
On the mirror surface, same size

explanation: At C the image returns to C, real, inverted, equal in size.

stem: A concave mirror of focal length 15 cm forms an image of an object placed 20 cm in front. Using the sign convention, the image distance v is:

options.text: -60 cm, so the image is 60 cm in front of the mirror
+60 cm, so the image is 60 cm behind the mirror
+30 cm, since f equals R

explanation: With u = -20 and f = -15, 1/v = 1/f - 1/u = -1/15 + 1/20 = -1/60, giving v = -60 cm: real, in front.

stem: For a convex mirror, which statement about the signs is correct for a real object?

options.text: u is negative while f and v are positive
All of u, v and f are positive
All of u, v and f are negative
f is negative because the mirror curves outward

explanation: Distances measured against the incident light are negative; a convex mirror's focus and virtual image lie behind it, so f and v are positive.

stem: A mirror produces a magnification of -3 for a 2 cm object. The image is:

options.text: 6 cm tall and inverted
About 0.67 cm tall and inverted
6 cm tall and erect
2 cm tall and inverted

explanation: The modulus of m gives the size ratio (3x, so 6 cm); the minus sign means inverted.

stem: A convex mirror used as a vehicle rear-view mirror gives a magnification of +0.5. The image is:

options.text: Erect and half the size of the object
Inverted and half the size
Erect and twice the size
The same size but reversed

explanation: Positive m means erect; 0.5 means half the size, which is why convex mirrors give a wide field of view.

stem: Light passes from air into water. What actually causes it to change direction?

options.text: Its speed changes at the boundary between the media
It bounces off the water surface
Its speed is the same but the water pushes it sideways
Water particles absorb and re-emit it randomly

explanation: Refraction arises because light travels at different speeds in different media.

stem: A ray travels from air into a glass block, striking the surface obliquely. It bends:

options.text: Toward the normal, because glass is optically denser
Away from the normal, because glass is optically denser
Not at all, since its speed is unchanged
Back into the air along the same path

explanation: Entering a denser medium light slows and bends toward the normal.

stem: The refractive index of water is 1.33. The speed of light in water is about:

options.text: 3 x 10^8 m/s, the same as in air

explanation: v = c/n = 3 x 10^8 / 1.33, which is about 2.26 x 10^8 m/s.

stem: What is the unit of refractive index?

options.text: It has no unit
m/s
dioptre
metre

explanation: It is the ratio of two speeds, so the units cancel.

stem: Light goes from glass (n = 1.5) into air. Compared with the incident ray, the refracted ray:

options.text: Bends away from the normal
Bends toward the normal
Continues undeviated regardless of the angle
Is reflected back into the glass at every angle

explanation: Going into a rarer medium light speeds up and bends away from the normal.

stem: A ray enters a medium at 45 degrees to the normal and refracts at 30 degrees. The refractive index is about:
explanation: n = sin 45 / sin 30 = 0.707 / 0.5, which is about 1.41.

stem: A ray passes obliquely through a rectangular glass slab. The emergent ray is:

options.text: Parallel to the incident ray but laterally displaced
Bent further away from the original direction
Reflected back along the incident path
Perpendicular to the incident ray

explanation: The two parallel surfaces produce equal and opposite bends, so direction is restored with a sideways shift.

stem: Lateral displacement through a glass slab increases when:

options.text: The slab is made thicker
The ray strikes exactly along the normal
The refractive index is reduced toward 1
The slab is cooled so light speeds up inside

explanation: Displacement grows with thickness, angle of incidence and refractive index; at normal incidence it is zero.

stem: Which lens is thicker at the middle than at the edges and converges a parallel beam?

options.text: Convex lens
Concave lens
Both converge a parallel beam
Neither, lenses only reflect light

explanation: A convex lens is thicker centrally and brings parallel rays to a real focus.

stem: Which statement about a convex lens is true?

options.text: It can form a diminished image when the object is beyond 2F
It always forms an enlarged image
It always forms a virtual image
It diverges every incident beam

explanation: Beyond 2F the image is real, inverted and diminished; magnification depends on object position.

stem: An object is at 2F of a convex lens. The image is:

options.text: At 2F on the other side, real, inverted and the same size
At F, real, inverted and enlarged
At infinity
Virtual and erect on the same side

explanation: Object at 2F gives an image at 2F, equal in size and inverted.

stem: An object is placed between F and the optical centre of a convex lens. The image is:

options.text: Virtual, erect and enlarged, on the same side as the object
Real, inverted and enlarged on the far side
Real and diminished at F
Always the same size as the object

explanation: This is the magnifying glass case: rays diverge after the lens, so the image is virtual, erect and magnified.

stem: A convex lens of focal length 10 cm has an object 15 cm away. The image distance v is:

options.text: +30 cm, real and on the opposite side
-30 cm, virtual and on the same side
+6 cm
+25 cm

stem: For the lens above, the magnification is -2. This means the image is:

options.text: Twice as tall as the object and inverted
Half as tall and inverted
Twice as tall and erect
The same height but reversed left to right

explanation: m = v/u = 30/(-15) = -2, so twice the size and inverted.

stem: A convex lens has a focal length of 20 cm. Its power is:
explanation: P = 1/f with f in metres: 1/0.20 = +5 D.

stem: Two thin lenses of powers +4 D and -6 D are placed in contact. The combination is:

options.text: A diverging lens of focal length about 50 cm
A converging lens of focal length about 10 cm
A diverging lens of power -24 D
A converging lens of power +0.02 D

explanation: Powers add: P = 4 - 6 = -2 D, so f = -0.5 m, a diverging combination of focal length 50 cm.
